subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 5 periods = 200 minutes
Total: 5 periods · 3h 20min

periods.activity_title: Faces, Edges, Corners: Meeting Solid Shapes

tasks_in_class.description: Use old boxes (cubes and cuboids) and bottles (cylinders) to do craft work. Draw faces on them. What did you draw on their faces?
Jaya's rocket: identify shapes used, count each type; answer which shape is between red and yellow cuboid, on top of orange cylinder, under pink cone.

time_bands.activity: Distribute collected boxes and bottles — one set per pair. Children handle each object, run fingers along its faces and edges, and count corners aloud. Teacher introduces the words face, edge, and corner by pointing to each feature on a cube held up for the class, then children do the same on their own objects. Let us Do, p.9 ("Use old boxes and bottles to do craft work....") follows: children draw animal or human faces on the flat faces of their boxes and curved surfaces of bottles, naming which shape they are decorating.

Teacher displays or sketches Jaya's rocket from Let us Do, p.9 ("Jaya's rocket: identify shapes used, count each type....") on the board. Children study the picture, name each solid shape they can spot, and count how many of each type appear. Pairs then discuss and write their counts before sharing with the class.

Using the same rocket picture, children answer the positional questions from Let us Do, p.9: which shape sits between the red and yellow cuboid, which sits on top of the orange cylinder, and which sits under the pink cone. Teacher calls on volunteers to point to their answer on the board and say the position word aloud, reinforcing the spatial vocabulary in full sentences.

periods.teacher_notes: Children at this stage often use a shape's everyday name (box, tin) rather than the geometric name; accept both initially and gently echo the geometric term. The labelled diagram of a cube showing face, edge, and corner is the visual anchor for this unit — keep it visible throughout. Watch for children who say a cylinder has corners: ask them to trace where the faces meet and feel whether a sharp corner is really there.
materials: Old cardboard boxes (cubes and cuboids), at least one per pair
Plastic bottles or cylindrical tins (cylinders)
Markers or crayons for drawing faces
A cone-shaped object (ice-cream cone wrapper or party hat) for display
Chalk or whiteboard marker for sketching the rocket diagram

periods.activity_title: Shapes Inside Shapes: The Toy Engine Hunt

tasks_in_class.description: Count and fill: how many red cylinders, yellow cones, grey cuboids, blue cubes in Devika's toy engine.
What shapes are used in these toys? (dog, lollipop, cat, block-set toy images)
Collect objects to make a house; name shapes, talk about faces and edges (straight/curved); describe arrangement; what part of shapes can you see from a distance?

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws or displays Devika's toy engine from Let us Do, p.10 ("Count and fill: how many red cylinders, yellow cones...."). Children study the image quietly, then fill the count table independently. After a brief pair-check, the class builds the counts together on the board, reinforcing each shape name as it is recorded.

Teacher shows the toy images from Let us Discuss, p.10 ("What shapes are used in these toys?...") — dog, lollipop, cat, block set. Small groups discuss which solid shapes they can spot in each toy. Groups share their reasoning: 'the lollipop has a sphere on a cylinder.' Teacher records shape names on the board and introduces the note that a cube is a special kind of cuboid.

Children work in groups on Let us Discuss, p.10 ("Collect objects to make a house; name shapes, talk about faces and edges...."). Each group assembles an available collection of boxes, bottles, and cones into a simple house or tower, names every shape used, and describes whether each face is flat or curved and each edge straight or curved. One member from each group presents their construction to the class, using position words to explain how shapes are arranged.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who can name shapes by colour or position from the engine image but cannot yet state why a shape is a cube rather than a cuboid are still working at the recognition level — guide them to count and compare faces. The cube-is-a-special-cuboid idea is introduced here through discussion rather than rule-giving; simply ask 'Are all the faces the same size on this box? On this one?' and let the class notice the difference. Keep the built house or tower intact on a desk for reference within this unit.
materials: Textbook open to p.10 or a projected image of Devika's toy engine
Assorted boxes, bottles, cones, and cylindrical objects (one set per group)
Pencils and exercise books for the count-and-fill table

periods.activity_title: Describe It, Build It: Sorting by What Shapes Have

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Play (Construct and Describe), p.11
tasks_in_class.description: In groups: one student selects 3 shapes, assembles them, describes the sequence; others build the same without seeing the original. Take turns.
Find classroom objects shaped like cylinder/sphere/cube/cuboid/cone; fill table; name shape found most and least; name objects made of more than one shape.
Name shapes: with no edges; with only flat faces; with only curved faces; with both straight and curved edges; with both flat and curved faces.

homework.description: Circle the cubes; tick the cones; cross the cylinders; draw a box around the cuboids (from a mixed group of shape images).

time_bands.activity: Groups play Construct and Describe from Let us Play, p.11 ("In groups: one student selects 3 shapes, assembles them, describes the sequence...."). The describer may not name the shape directly — only describe using face and edge language ('it has only flat faces', 'it has a curved surface at the bottom'). Listeners build the sequence from available solid objects or blocks. Groups swap the describer role at least twice so every child practises the language.

Children complete Let us Do Q1, p.11 ("Find classroom objects shaped like cylinder/sphere/cube/cuboid/cone; fill table....") individually or in pairs. They walk the room, record one real object per shape in their table, then return to answer: which shape appears most around the classroom, which least, and which objects are built from more than one shape. Pairs compare findings and discuss any disagreements.

Teacher poses the property questions from Let us Do Q3, p.12 ("Name shapes: with no edges; with only flat faces....") one at a time to the whole class. For each property, children hold up a matching solid object and justify their choice: 'a sphere has no edges because there is no line where two faces meet.' Teacher compiles the class answers in a simple two-column list on the board — property on the left, shape name on the right — as an emerging classification chart.

periods.teacher_notes: The Construct and Describe game is the central act of this unit: it forces children to move from visual recognition to property language, which is the shift the section is building. A common error in Q3 is naming a cone as having 'only flat faces' — invite the child to run a finger around the cone's surface to feel the curved part before deciding. Let us Do Q2 (p.12) — circling, ticking, and crossing shape images — is set as an independent practice task for after the unit; note it for children who need additional reinforcement.
materials: Sets of solid shape objects or blocks — at least one cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone per group
Textbook open to pp.11–12
Pencils and rulers for filling the table and marking Q2

periods.activity_title: Clay, Sticks, and Cubes: Constructing and Comparing Solids

tasks_in_class.description: Which shapes can you build? Make shapes using clay and sticks (cube-skeleton and octahedron-skeleton shown as examples).
In what ways are these shapes (cylinder, cube, cuboid, cone, sphere) the same? In what ways are they different?
Look at a die (faces 1–6). What number is on the face opposite 1? Opposite 2? Opposite 3? What pattern do you notice?

homework.description: Try to make the given shapes using cubes (two example cube-block configurations shown).

time_bands.activity: Children work in pairs on Let us Do Q4, p.13 ("Which shapes can you build? Make shapes using clay and sticks...."). Each pair receives a small lump of clay and a handful of sticks cut to equal lengths. They first build a cube skeleton — four sticks per layer, joined at corners with clay — then attempt other shapes. Teacher circulates, asking: 'How many sticks does your cube need? How many corner joints?' Children record their shape names and stick counts in their books.

Teacher places a cylinder, cube, cuboid, cone, and sphere (or pictures of them) at the front. The class works through Let us Do Q6, p.14 ("In what ways are these shapes the same? In what ways are they different?...") as a guided whole-class discussion. Teacher records a simple comparison in two columns — 'same' and 'different' — on the board, drawing out face type, edge type, and presence or absence of corners.

Each child picks up a die and examines it for Let us Do Q7, p.14 ("Look at a die. What number is on the face opposite 1?..."). Children record the opposite-face pairs in their books, then the teacher asks: 'What do you notice about each pair?' Children share observations until the 1+6, 2+5, 3+4 pattern is named. Teacher asks: 'Does this work for any die? Let us check with a neighbour's die.'

periods.teacher_notes: The clay-and-sticks task reveals whether children understand that a skeleton captures edges and corners but not faces — some will try to fill in the faces with clay; use this as a discussion point rather than a correction. In the comparison discussion for Q6, children often say shapes are 'the same' because they are all 3D; press further with 'can you roll it? can you stack it?' to surface property differences. The pattern on the die (opposite faces sum to seven) is the conceptual goal of Q7; let children state it in their own words before the teacher names it.
materials: Modelling clay or playdough (small portion per pair)
Sticks or toothpicks cut to equal lengths (about 20 per pair)
One standard die per child or per pair
Solid shape objects or pictures for the comparison discussion
Exercise books and pencils

periods.activity_title: All the Ways: Joining Cubes and Playing the Shape Game

tasks_in_class.description: In what order is this model built? (table-like model with cuboid base, cylinder supports, and cone tops)
In how many different ways can you join 3 cubes? What shape do you get if you join a cube and a cuboid? How many cubes make the given shape?
Name the shapes used in models (a)(b)(c)(d). Describe how the shapes are arranged.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Play (Shape Board Game), p.12–13
tasks_in_class.description: Roll die, move counter to next picture matching number's shape (1=Cylinder, 2=Sphere, 3=Cone, 4=Cube, 5=Cuboid, 6=Move 2 forward). First to Finish wins.

homework.description: Use six dice to make: (a) a cuboid (b) a tower (c) any other shape of your choice.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the table-like model from Let us Do Q8, p.14 ("In what order is this model built?...") on the board. Children study it and write the build sequence — which piece goes first, second, third — in their books, explaining why that order is necessary. A brief class share-out checks whether children reason about stability (base before supports before tops).

Each child receives three unit cubes. They work through Let us Do Q9, p.15 ("In how many different ways can you join 3 cubes?..."), physically arranging the cubes and sketching each distinct configuration. Teacher circulates asking: 'Is this arrangement really different from that one, or just rotated?' Class pools all unique arrangements on the board. Children then place a cube next to a small cuboid box and describe the combined shape.

Teacher shows the four models from Let us Do Q10, p.15 ("Name the shapes used in models (a)(b)(c)(d)...."). Children name every solid shape they can see in each model and describe the spatial arrangement — 'a cylinder is on top of the cuboid, a cone sits on top of the cylinder.' Pairs compare descriptions and settle on agreed answers.

Children play the Shape Board Game from Let us Play, p.12–13 ("Roll die, move counter to next picture matching number's shape....") in groups of three or four. Each roll requires naming the target shape before moving. Teacher observes for fluent shape naming and prompt recall. Let us Do Q11, p.15 — building shapes from six dice — is introduced as an activity to try at home, with a quick demonstration of how six dice can be stacked into a cuboid.

periods.teacher_notes: Children frequently think that two three-cube arrangements are different simply because they drew them differently on paper — use the physical cubes to rotate and superimpose, showing that orientation does not create a new arrangement. The sequencing question for Q8 grounds abstract spatial reasoning in a concrete stability argument: the base must be laid before anything can be placed on top. The board game gives a quick informal check of whether all five shape names are now available to every child; note any child who hesitates so that additional naming practice can be offered.
materials: Three unit cubes per child (wooden or plastic blocks)
Small cuboid box per pair (for the cube-plus-cuboid combination)
Shape Board Game from pp.12–13 (one copy per group, or textbook shared)
One die per group for the board game
Counters or small objects as playing pieces
Exercise books and pencils

tasks.description: Roll die, move counter to next picture matching number's shape (1=Cylinder, 2=Sphere, 3=Cone, 4=Cube, 5=Cuboid, 6=Move 2 forward). First to Finish wins.

items.prompt: Pick up a cylindrical tin. Run your finger along its surfaces. How many flat faces does it have? Does it have any curved surface? How many edges can you feel where the flat and curved surfaces meet?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A cylinder has 2 flat faces (the circular top and bottom) and 1 curved surface. It has 2 edges, one at the top and one at the bottom, where the flat faces meet the curved surface.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Handle the object and count each type of surface and each edge where surfaces meet.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: let the child trace each surface with a finger before answering; stretch: ask whether a cone has the same number of flat faces and why.

exercise.description: Use old boxes (cubes and cuboids) and bottles (cylinders) to do craft work. Draw faces on them. What did you draw on their faces?

items.prompt: Look around your classroom. Write the name of one object that looks like a cylinder, one that looks like a cuboid, and one that looks like a cone. For each object, write whether its faces are flat, curved, or both.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Accepted examples — cylinder: chalk, water bottle (curved surface + 2 flat circular faces); cuboid: textbook, chalk box (all flat faces); cone: party hat, sharpened pencil tip (1 flat face + 1 curved surface). Answers will vary; marking is on correct face-type description for the named object.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Match each classroom object to its solid shape, then state whether its surfaces are flat, curved, or both.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: let the child hold the actual object and feel the surfaces before writing; stretch: ask the child to name one object made of more than one shape and describe each part.

exercise.description: Find classroom objects shaped like cylinder/sphere/cube/cuboid/cone; fill table; name shape found most and least; name objects made of more than one shape.

items.prompt: Priya places a cube on the table, then puts a cylinder on top of it, and finally rests a cone on top of the cylinder. She removes the shape that is between the cube and the cone. Which shape does she remove?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Cylinder. It sits between the cube (below) and the cone (above), so it is the shape in the middle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the positional description — between the cube and the cone — and identify which shape occupies that position in the stack.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child has confused 'between' with 'at the bottom'; they may not yet link the word 'between' to a middle position.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child has confused 'between' with 'on top'; they may be reading only the last shape named rather than the positional relationship.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child has not tracked the shapes described and has guessed a shape not mentioned in the arrangement.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: ask the child to act out the stack with real objects before answering; stretch: ask the child to describe a four-shape stack using between, on top of, and under in one sentence.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Play (Construct and Describe), p.11
exercise.description: In groups: one student selects 3 shapes, assembles them, describes the sequence; others build the same without seeing the original. Take turns.

items.prompt: You want to build a skeleton of a cube using sticks and clay. You need one stick for each edge. How many sticks do you need? How many clay balls (corner joints) do you need?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A cube has 12 edges, so 12 sticks are needed. It has 8 corners, so 8 clay balls are needed.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the edges and corners of a cube: 12 edges and 8 corners.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: let the child handle a real cube box and count edges by touching each one; stretch: ask how many sticks a cuboid skeleton would need and whether it is the same as the cube.

exercise.description: Which shapes can you build? Make shapes using clay and sticks (cube-skeleton and octahedron-skeleton shown as examples).

items.prompt: Take 3 cubes of the same size. Join them so that each cube touches at least one full face of another cube. Draw or describe two different arrangements you can make. Are the two arrangements truly different, or is one just a rotation of the other?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: With 3 cubes joined face-to-face, there are 2 truly different arrangements: a straight line (all three in a row) and an L-shape (two in a row with the third turning at a right angle). A bent row that can be rotated to look like a straight row counts as the same arrangement.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Physically arrange the cubes, then rotate the arrangement to check whether it matches another — if it does after rotation, it is not a new arrangement.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: provide the physical cubes and let the child build before describing; stretch: ask how many arrangements are possible with 4 cubes and whether the child can find them all.

exercise.description: In how many different ways can you join 3 cubes? What shape do you get if you join a cube and a cuboid? How many cubes make the given shape?

items.prompt: Ria builds a rocket. She places a cone directly on top of a cylinder. The cylinder rests on a cuboid. Which shape is between the cuboid and the cone?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Cylinder. The cuboid is at the base, the cone is at the top, and the cylinder is sandwiched between them.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the stacking order from base to top — cuboid, then cylinder, then cone — and identify the middle shape.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child has introduced a shape not present in the description, suggesting they guessed without tracking the arrangement.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child may be confusing a cube with the cylinder or have misread 'cuboid' as the middle shape.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child has selected the topmost shape rather than the one in the middle, showing uncertainty about the meaning of 'between'.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: ask the child to stack three objects on a desk as described, then point to the middle one; stretch: ask what position the cuboid is in relative to the cylinder and the table.

exercise.description: Jaya's rocket: identify shapes used, count each type; answer which shape is between red and yellow cuboid, on top of orange cylinder, under pink cone.

items.prompt: Kavya says: 'My shape has no edges at all.' Which shape could she be holding? Now Arjun says: 'My shape has both flat faces and a curved face.' Name one shape Arjun could be holding. Explain how you decided.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Kavya holds a sphere — it has no edges because its entire surface is one continuous curved surface with no lines where two faces meet. Arjun holds a cylinder or a cone — both have at least one flat face and a curved surface. The child should name one and explain: for example, a cylinder has two flat circular faces and one curved surface, so it fits Arjun's clue.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Match each clue to the shape whose face and edge properties satisfy it exactly.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: let the child hold a sphere and a cylinder while reading the clues, feeling for edges; stretch: ask the child to write a new clue for a cube that uses only face and edge words.

exercise.description: Name shapes: with no edges; with only flat faces; with only curved faces; with both straight and curved edges; with both flat and curved faces.

items.prompt: Look at a cube and a sphere. Write one way they are the same and one way they are different. Now look at a cylinder and a cone. Write one way they are the same and one way they are different.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Cube and sphere — same: both are three-dimensional solid shapes; different: a cube has flat faces and edges/corners, a sphere has only a curved surface and no edges or corners. Cylinder and cone — same: both have a curved surface and at least one flat circular face; different: a cylinder has two flat faces and a cone has only one flat face (or: a cone comes to a point, a cylinder does not).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare each pair on face type (flat or curved), presence of edges, and presence of corners.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: provide the physical objects and ask the child to feel one property at a time — 'find the flat faces first'; stretch: ask the child to find one property that is the same across all four shapes.

exercise.description: In what ways are these shapes (cylinder, cube, cuboid, cone, sphere) the same? In what ways are they different?

items.prompt: Meena looks at a standard die. She finds that the face with 4 dots is opposite the face with 3 dots. Her friend says: 'That cannot be right on a standard die.' Who is correct? What number should be opposite 4 on a standard die, and how do you know?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Meena's friend is correct. On a standard die, opposite faces always add up to 7. So the face opposite 4 must be 3 (because 4 + 3 = 7). Since 3 is opposite 4, Meena's die either is non-standard or she has misread it.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the opposite-faces pattern: each pair of opposite faces on a standard die sums to 7, so the face opposite 4 is 7 minus 4, which equals 3.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: give the child a real die to check each opposite pair and record the sums before answering; stretch: ask what number would be opposite 4 if the rule were 'opposite faces sum to 8' and whether such a die is possible with faces 1–6.

exercise.description: Look at a die (faces 1–6). What number is on the face opposite 1? Opposite 2? Opposite 3? What pattern do you notice?

items.prompt: A toy train has 3 cylinders, 2 cuboids, 1 cube, and 2 cones. How many shapes are used in the toy train altogether?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the counts of each shape type: 3 cylinders + 2 cuboids + 1 cube + 2 cones = 8 shapes.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child has counted only 4 types of shapes (one for each shape name) plus 3, suggesting they counted types rather than individual shapes and then added just one group.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child has likely made an addition error, possibly counting one group twice or adding an extra 1.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child has counted only the number of different shape types (4) plus 2, or has missed one group entirely.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: ask the child to write each shape count separately and point to each number before adding; stretch: ask which shape type appears most and how many more cylinders there are than cones.

exercise.description: Count and fill: how many red cylinders, yellow cones, grey cuboids, blue cubes in Devika's toy engine.

items.prompt: In the Shape Board Game, a player rolls a 3. According to the game rules, the player must move to the next picture that shows which shape?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Cone. In the game, 3 corresponds to a cone.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the game's number-to-shape rule: 1 = Cylinder, 2 = Sphere, 3 = Cone, 4 = Cube, 5 = Cuboid.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child has recalled the rule for 1, not 3, suggesting confusion between adjacent number-shape pairings.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child has recalled the rule for 4, not 3, suggesting a shift of one in the sequence.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child has recalled the rule for 5, not 3, suggesting uncertainty about which number maps to which shape.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: let the child refer to the game board and trace the number-shape list before answering; stretch: ask what shape the player would move to if they rolled a 5, and then what happens if they roll a 6.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Play (Shape Board Game), p.12–13
exercise.description: Roll die, move counter to next picture matching number's shape (1=Cylinder, 2=Sphere, 3=Cone, 4=Cube, 5=Cuboid, 6=Move 2 forward). First to Finish wins.
